svg.title: B+ high-voltage DC supply path through the ST-70
svg.desc: From the PA-060 HV secondary through the 5AR4 rectifier and a multi-stage filter network (choke + three RC stages), out to every tube plate and screen. Voltages cascade downward and ripple decreases with each stage.
svg.text: B+ supply — from rectifier to every plate
Each stage drops the voltage AND smooths it. By the time B+ reaches the input stage it's ~30 dB cleaner than what came off the rectifier cathode.

g.data-tooltip:
PA-060 HV SECONDARY — center-tapped winding.
Two red leads at the ends of the winding, red/yellow CT in the middle. Across the full winding, 720 V RMS AC (360-0-360) at 60 Hz. From either red lead to the CT, ~510 Vp (~360 Vrms), shifted 180° between the two halves.
This is the only AC stage in the B+ path — everything downstream is DC after rectification.

5AR4 RECTIFIER — full-wave dual-anode.
Each anode (pins 4 and 6) conducts on alternate half-cycles — 60 times per second each, so together they deliver 120 pulses per second. The cathode (pin 8) sees a positive pulse on every half-cycle: pulsating DC at 120 Hz.
Optional MOD: a 1N4007 in series with each plate provides arc-protection for the rectifier tube. See modifications/rectifier-diode-mod.

FILTER CAP — lug 2, first stage (~30 µF).
This cap starts smoothing the pulsating DC: it absorbs current on the peak of each 120 Hz pulse and releases current between pulses. The result is DC with significant ripple (~20-30 Vpp of 120 Hz on top of the ~435 V average).
Wired in step 29: V1 pin 8 → cap lug 2.

CHOKE — inductor (~1.5 H, ~100 Ω DC resistance).
The choke resists rapid changes in current — together with the cap on lug 1 downstream, it forms an LC low-pass filter that removes essentially all of the 120 Hz ripple.
Some DC voltage drops across the choke's resistance (the steady current × 100 Ω ≈ 20 V drop at typical idle).

FILTER CAP — lug 1, second stage (~20 µF).
After the choke, ripple is reduced by ~30 dB. This is the clean B+ rail that feeds the output transformer primaries — both A-470 red leads (center taps) land here in step 8.
Push-pull operation in the output stage further cancels what little ripple remains.

A-470 PRIMARY CENTER TAPS — both channels feed from this single B+ node.
The red leads of both A-470 output transformers land on cap lug 1. Push-pull operation means the two halves of each primary draw equal-but-opposite AC currents, so the DC load on B+ is steady; this rejects whatever 120 Hz ripple remains.
g.text: both channels — EL34 plates + UL screens

g.data-tooltip:
6.8 kΩ DROPPING RESISTOR — between cap lug 1 and cap lug 4.
Together with the cap on lug 4, forms an RC filter that drops the voltage and smooths it further. The voltage drop across the resistor depends on the current draw of everything downstream — typically ~40 V at idle.
Wired in step 30.

FILTER CAP — lug 4, third stage (~20 µF).
Output of this stage feeds the PC-3A driver board via eyelet 19. The 6GH8A TRIODE-section plate loads connect here through their plate resistors.
By now ripple is dramatically reduced — the driver stage barely sees any.

6GH8A PENTODE SCREENS + TRIODE PLATES — fed from cap lug 4 via PC-3A eyelet 20 (step 43).
The pentode screen grids get this voltage through an on-board screen-dropping resistor. The triode (cathodyne phase splitter) plate loads also feed from here. Both want a moderately clean rail at ~375 V.

22 kΩ + CAP LUG 3 — final filter stage.
22 kΩ dropping resistor (step 42) between lug 4 and lug 3, plus the cap on lug 3, form the last RC filter. Both the resistor and the cap are mounted on the FILTER CAP CHASSIS — not on the PC-3A board.
This is the cleanest, lowest-voltage B+ rail (~305 V). Delivered to the PC-3A pentode plate-load via eyelet 19.

6GH8A PENTODE PLATE LOAD — input voltage amplifier feed.
Fed from cap lug 3 via PC-3A eyelet 19 (step 41). The pentode plates are at the front of the gain chain; any 120 Hz ripple here gets multiplied by ~50× (pentode) × ~50× (triode) × push-pull gain and lands as audible hum. So this rail gets the most filtering and the lowest voltage in the cascade.

HV CENTER TAP — return path for both halves of the rectified AC.
The red/yellow CT lands at the filter cap ground (step 7), establishing the reference that makes B+ a 'positive' voltage relative to chassis ground. Without this, the rectifier loop wouldn't close.

svg.text: Each cascade stage drops voltage (via choke or resistor) AND smooths it (via the cap on the next lug). Cleaner rails for higher-gain stages.
Approximate idle voltages; see voltage-checks for bring-up targets.
